title: A CMU software-engineering professor rebuilt his course around oral check-ins because agents could do every assignment, and now assumes AI tool fluency as a baseline
summary:
Christian Kästner, who teaches Machine Learning in Production at Carnegie Mellon to 100 to 170 students a term, reports that AI agents could complete all of his assignments and that he has redesigned most of his assessment. Written reflections were replaced by 15-minute check-ins with a teaching assistant, in which students defend their answers orally and take follow-up questions. Graded reading quizzes were dropped, coding assignments were scaled up to projects that current agents do not solve without guidance, and the exam's share of the grade rose from 15% to 25%. LLM-based grading with human review before any penalty cut teaching-assistant grading time by 50 to 80%.

Two consequences reach beyond the classroom. Kästner now treats competence with AI coding tools as a baseline he assumes, as he previously assumed basic programming, so graduates arrive expecting to work with agents. And he says AI is pushing him away from evidence-based practice, frequent low-stakes assessment with feedback, towards fewer high-stakes checks, and that the pace of redesign is accelerating each term.

For employers the parallel is direct. Take-home work no longer shows what a candidate understands, and the remedy Kästner reached, a short oral defence of work that may have been machine-produced, is one hiring and internal skills assessment can adopt.
observer: Christian Kästner, professor at Carnegie Mellon University's software engineering programme, who teaches the upper-level course Machine Learning in Production to 100-170 students per term and describes changes he made to his own course.
leadTimeEstimate: ~12-24 months before this cohort's expectations and the oral-defence assessment pattern show up in hiring practice
whyItMatters: **Written work no longer shows understanding** — if agents complete the assignments, a take-home test or code sample says little about what a candidate knows.
**Oral defence becomes the check** — a short conversation about work the candidate may not have written is what a leading programme settled on.
**Graduates assume agent fluency** — a course that treats AI tool use as a baseline produces hires who expect agents in their workflow from the first day.
**Feedback-rich learning is under pressure** — the practices that build skill fastest are the ones AI undermines, which carries into on-the-job training too.
risksAndCaveats: **One course, one instructor** — this is a single firsthand account and has not been independently validated or compared with other programmes.
**No learning-outcome data** — Kästner says he lacks rigorous evidence on whether students learn more or less, and grade drift predates the changes.
